summary: A 1975 note discussing how the FTP CWD command should work for login access to directories that only hold files. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: The note asks what should happen when you change folders on a remote computer, and the folder is one you may only look at.

subtitle: Should FTP allow password-protected directory access?

tldr.problem: TENEX FTP servers do not allow FTP login to "files only" directories. Users cannot access private file directories with owner privileges because CWD (Change Working Directory) does not grant owner access.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal is to either allow FTP logins to files-only directories, or add an optional password argument to the CWD command that grants ownership rights if the password matches.
tldr.outcome: The note outlines the trade-off: allowing FTP logins requires accepting that any network user knowing the password has ownership status in FTP, or adding a CWD password mechanism to maintain restriction.

today: RFC 697 is a design question from the early TENEX community about how FTP should handle privileged directory access. It remains relevant to discussions of authentication and access control in file transfer protocols.

sections.title: Directory Access in TENEX FTP
sections.content:
TENEX has two types of directories: normal directories that can be "logged into" with owner access, and "files only" directories that can be "connected to" but not logged into. Logging into a directory gives the user (the job and its address space) owner access under TENEX's protection model. Connecting to a directory allows access to files without creating a new address space.

The TENEX FTP server currently allows login to normal directories but not to files-only directories. This means a user cannot access a files-only directory with owner privileges using FTP, only with the public or group protection levels that TENEX assigns by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Some folders on TENEX are set up so you cannot "log in" to them through the file transfer program, even if you know the password.

sections.title: The Problem and Two Approaches
sections.content:
For private files-only directories, users either need to rely on restrictive group protection (which is cumbersome if only a few directories need it) or accept unrestricted public access (which is undesirable for private data). The note identifies two ways to solve this:

Option 1: Remove the restriction. Allow FTP login to files-only directories. This treats any network user who knows the password as an owner of that directory within FTP.

Option 2: Add a password mechanism to CWD. Extend the CWD command with an optional password argument. If the password is provided and matches, the user gains owner access. If no password is given or the password fails, CWD works as it currently does with standard protection rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Either let people log in to locked folders with a password, or add a special command that opens them. The choice depends on how strict you want security to be.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.content: Option 1 is simpler but less secure: it assumes that knowing the directory password is equivalent to being the directory owner. Option 2 is more restrictive: it gives users access to the directory's contents via CWD but does not change their ownership status in the broader system. The note notes that anonymous users should not be allowed to use a password mechanism to elevate their access.
sections.plainLanguage: Option 1 is easy but trusts the network. Option 2 is more careful but more complex to implement.
